title: Wilson's Theorem: Complete Classification for Non-Prime Moduli
description: Extends Wilson's theorem to all moduli n≥2: for composite n>4, n∣(n-1)!; for n=4, (n-1)! ≡ 2 (mod 4); for primes, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p). Formalizes Wilson primes (p∣(p-1)!+1 with p²), verifies 5, 13 are Wilson primes, and proves the Gauss-Wilson classification (product of units ≡ -1 iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}). 33 theorems, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Wilson's theorem was discovered by John Wilson around 1770 and first proved by Joseph-Louis Lagrange in 1773. The statement — (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) iff p is prime — provides an exact characterization of primality via factorials, though it is computationally impractical as a primality test. The natural generalization asks: what is (n-1)! mod n for composite n? The answer turns out to be a clean trichotomy: 0 for composite n > 4, exactly 2 for n = 4, and -1 for primes. This was known to Gauss by 1801. The deeper Gauss-Wilson theorem classifies when the product of all units mod n equals -1: this happens exactly when (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic, i.e., when n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k} for odd prime p. Gauss proved this via his theory of primitive roots. Wilson primes — primes p where p² | (p-1)!+1 — were likely observed in the 19th century. The known Wilson primes are 5 (discovered that 4!+1=25=5²), 13 (verified computationally), and 563 (found by Goldberg in 1953 by machine computation). No fourth Wilson prime is known; a search has been completed up to roughly 2×10¹³. The connection to Bernoulli numbers (p Wilson prime iff p | B_{p-1}) links them to Kummer's theory of regular primes and Fermat's Last Theorem.
overview.problemStatement: Classify (n-1)! mod n for all n≥2. Formalize Wilson primes. Prove the Gauss-Wilson classification of n where ∏units ≡ -1.
overview.text: Three cases: (1) If p is prime, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) by pairing each a with its inverse, except a = ±1. (2) If n = 4, 3! = 6 ≡ 2 (mod 4) — the unique exception. (3) If n is composite and n > 4, then n | (n-1)! because n = a·b with distinct a,b < n both appearing in (n-1)!. The Gauss-Wilson theorem: ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}.
overview.proofStrategy: Prove the three cases of Wilson's theorem directly. Define Wilson quotient and Wilson primes. Use Mathlib's isCyclic_units_iff_gaussWilson for the classification. Verify specific small cases by native_decide.
keyInsights: Composite n>4: n = a·b with a≠b, both in {1,...,n-1}; for n=p² (p≥3) use p and 2p instead
n=4 is uniquely exceptional: the only composite where (n-1)! is neither 0 nor -1 mod n
Wilson quotient W_p = ((p-1)!+1)/p is always a positive integer; Wilson prime requires p | W_p
Gauss-Wilson ↔ cyclic unit group: (ℤ/nℤ)* cyclic iff exactly 2 self-inverse units iff product = -1
Self-inverse pairing argument: non-self-inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹) cancel; only ±1 remain in cyclic case
Mathlib bridge: ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff provides the full p^k/2p^k characterization, used via OQ02
prerequisites: Wilson's theorem for primes: pairing inverses

conclusion.summary: Wilson's theorem fully generalized: trichotomy (n-1)! ≡ {-1, 2, 0} mod n for primes, n=4, composite n>4 respectively. Wilson quotient, Wilson primes defined; 5 and 13 verified. Gauss-Wilson classification proved for all n≥3 via Mathlib's ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff and OQ02's abstract bridge. Computationally verified to n≤200. 33 theorems, 9 definitions, 688 lines, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: The Gauss-Wilson classification is the number-theoretic foundation for primitive root theory and cyclic unit groups in algebraic number theory. It implies: primitive roots exist mod n iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}. Wilson primes connect to irregular primes, Bernoulli numbers, and Kummer's proof strategy for Fermat's Last Theorem. The only known Wilson primes are 5, 13, and 563; this remains a major open problem.
openQuestions: Are there infinitely many Wilson primes? — equivalent to asking if p | B_{p-1} for infinitely many primes p
Formalize the third Wilson prime 563 (12-digit native_decide verification would require efficient arbitrary-precision arithmetic)
Prove or disprove: p is Wilson prime iff p | B_{p-1} — formalize the Bernoulli number connection in Lean
Formalize the Gauss-Wilson theorem without relying on ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff (direct involution-product proof)
